tasks.description: Create an integer variable `age` with value 30. Print its type using type().
tasks.hint:
`type(value)` returns the data type of any value — very useful for debugging.
Wrap it inside print: `print(type(age))`
Integers display as `<class 'int'>` — this is Python's way of naming the type.
tasks.walkthrough:
`30` has no decimal point and no quotes, so Python stores it as an int.
`type(age)` looks up that type, and printing it shows `<class 'int'>`.

tasks.description: Create a float variable `price = 19.99`. Print it rounded to the nearest whole number.
tasks.hint:
`round(value)` with no second argument rounds to the nearest whole number.
`round(19.99)` → `20`, `round(19.49)` → `19`
Common pitfall: `round()` returns an int when rounding to 0 places, so the output is `20` not `20.0`.
tasks.walkthrough:
`round()` with just one argument rounds to the nearest whole number.
19.99 is closest to 20, and because no decimal places were asked for, the result is the int `20`.

tasks.description: Create a string variable `city = 'paris'`. Print it converted to ALL UPPERCASE.
tasks.hint:
Strings have built-in methods you call with a dot: `variable.method()`
`.upper()` returns a NEW uppercase string — it does not modify the original.
`print(city.upper())` → `PARIS`
tasks.walkthrough:
`.upper()` is a method that belongs to strings. You call it with a dot after the variable.
It returns a new uppercase string, which goes straight into `print`.

tasks.description: Create a boolean variable `is_sunny = True`. Print the variable, then print its type on a new line.
tasks.hint:
Boolean values in Python are `True` and `False` — capital first letter is required.
Two separate `print()` calls: first `print(is_sunny)`, then `print(type(is_sunny))`
Boolean type shows as `<class 'bool'>`.
tasks.walkthrough:
`True` with a capital T is one of Python's two boolean values.
The first print shows the value itself, the second shows its type, `<class 'bool'>`.

tasks.description: Print the type of each of these values on separate lines: 42, 3.14, 'hello', True
tasks.hint:
Call `print(type(...))` four times — you can pass the value directly without storing in a variable.
Order matters for matching the expected output: int, float, str, bool.
`print(type(42))` → `<class 'int'>`
tasks.walkthrough:
You can pass a value straight into `type()` without storing it in a variable first.
Whole number, decimal, quoted text, and True map to int, float, str and bool.
The order matters because the checker compares line by line.

tasks.description: The string '15' cannot be used for math. Convert it to an integer using int(), then add 5 and print the result.
tasks.hint:
`int('15')` converts the string `'15'` to the number `15` so you can do math with it.
You can do this in one expression: `print(int('15') + 5)`
Common error: `'15' + 5` raises a TypeError — Python won't mix strings and numbers.
tasks.walkthrough:
`int('15')` reads the characters and produces the number 15.
Now it's a real number, so `+ 5` does arithmetic and gives 20.
Without the conversion, Python would refuse to add a string and a number.

tasks.description: Create a variable `pi = 3.14159`. Print it, then print it rounded to 2 decimal places.
tasks.hint:
`round(value, n)` takes a second argument: the number of decimal places to keep.
`round(pi, 2)` → `3.14`
Use two separate `print()` calls: first the raw value, then the rounded one.
tasks.walkthrough:
The first print shows the full value as stored.
`round(pi, 2)` keeps two digits after the decimal point, giving `3.14`.
The second argument to `round` is how many decimal places to keep.

lesson.intro:
Every value in Python has a type: a whole number, a decimal, some text, or a
true/false. Most of the confusing errors you'll hit early on come from mixing
types up, so today is about learning to see them.

sections.heading: The four types you'll meet first
sections.body:
- `int` is a whole number like `30` or `-2`.
- `float` is a number with a decimal point like `19.99` or `5.0`.
- `str` is text, always in quotes, like `'paris'`.
- `bool` is either `True` or `False`, capital letter required.

You don't declare types. Python works out the type from what you write.
The `type()` function tells you what it decided.
sections.code:
age = 30
price = 19.99
city = 'paris'
is_sunny = True

print(type(age))
print(type(price))
print(type(city))
print(type(is_sunny))

sections.heading: Text that looks like a number is still text
sections.body:
`'15'` with quotes is a string, even though it looks like a number. You can't
do maths with it until you convert it. `int()` turns text into a whole number,
`float()` into a decimal, and `str()` turns a number back into text.

sections.heading: Strings come with built-in tools
sections.body:
Text values have methods you call with a dot. `.upper()` gives you an uppercase
copy, `.lower()` a lowercase one. They don't change the original; they hand you
a new string.

sections.heading: Rounding
sections.body:
`round(x)` rounds to the nearest whole number and gives you an int.
`round(x, 2)` keeps two decimal places and gives you a float.

watch_out: `'15' + 5` crashes with a TypeError. Python won't guess whether you want text or maths. Convert first.
`true` and `false` in lowercase aren't Python. It's `True` and `False`.
`city.upper()` doesn't change `city`. If you want to keep the result, assign it: `city = city.upper()`.
`round(19.99)` gives `20`, not `20.0`. Rounding to zero places returns an int.
